content: Phytolacca americana, commonly known as American pokeweed, is a large, shrubby perennial plant that can grow up to 10 feet in height. It is native to eastern North America. The plant is also referred to by various names, including American nightshade, cancer jalap, coakum, garget, inkberry, pigeon berry, pocan bush, poke root, pokeweed, redweed, scoke, red ink plant, and in Chinese medicine, chui xu shang lu. Despite its historical and medicinal uses, parts of the plant are highly toxic to both humans and livestock, and it is considered a significant pest plant by farmers. However, different parts of the plant, at various stages of growth, have been used as food, medicine, or poison. The plant features a large white taproot, green or red stems, and large, simple leaves. Its white flowers develop into purple to nearly black berries, which serve as a food source for songbirds such as the Northern Cardinal, Brown Thrasher, and Northern Mockingbird. Morphology Phytolacca americana is a perennial herbaceous plant that typically grows to a height of 4 feet but can reach up to 10 feet. The central stem is often red as the plant matures and may have one or more stalks. The plant dies back to its roots each winter. The leaves are alternate, coarse in texture, and moderately porous, reaching up to 9 inches in length and 2 inches in width. They are medium green, smooth, and emit an unpleasant odor. The flowers lack true petals but have white petal-like sepals on white pedicels and peduncles, arranged in upright or drooping racemes. The flowers bloom from early summer to early fall. The fruit is a shiny, dark purple berry held in racemous clusters on pink pedicels with a pink peduncle. Immature berries are green, turning white and then blackish-purple as they mature. The berries are pomes, round with a flat, indented top and bottom. The root is a thick central taproot that grows deep and spreads horizontally. It has a tan cortex, white pulp, and a moderate number of rootlets. When cut transversely, the root shows concentric rings. The plant does not fix nitrogen. Habitat and Range American pokeweed is widely distributed in fields and waste areas, often found in edge habitats. Birds that consume the berries help spread the seeds, which do not require stratification to germinate. The plant thrives in both sun and shade and can survive fire due to its robust root structure. In recent years, it has become more common in populated areas. It is found throughout most of the United States, except in the Mountain States, Alaska, and Hawaii. Known Constituents The plant contains triterpene saponins, including phytolaccosides A, B, C, D, E, F, and G, as well as phytolaccagenin, jaligonic acid, esculentic acid, and phytolaccagenic acid. Other constituents include triterpene alcohols such as alpha-spinasterol and its derivatives, phytolaccatoxin, canthomicrol, astragalin, protein PAP-R, mitogens (a series of glycoproteins), caryophylline, lectins, tannin, and starch. Oleanolic acid, a significant component, has demonstrated anticancer properties, particularly against various carcinomas and leukemia. Uses Traditional Medicinal Uses Historically, American pokeweed has been used to treat syphilis, diphtheria, conjunctivitis, cancer, adenitis, and emesis, or as a purgative. Topically, it has been applied for scabies. It is classified as a heroic and toxic herb, requiring professional training for safe use. A tincture of the root has been used as an alterative for lymphatic disorders, breast lumps, skin conditions, arthritis, rheumatism, conjunctivitis, tonsillitis, infectious diseases, edema, and cancer. Roasted root poultices have been applied to breast abscesses, rheumatic pains, and swellings. Root washes have been used for sprains and swellings, while root-infused oil has been employed in cancer protocols. The berries, when consumed without biting into the toxic seeds, have been used for arthritis. Berry juice has been applied topically for cancer, hemorrhoids, and tremors. The leaves, which are cathartic and purgative, have also been used medicinally. Modern Pharmacological Uses Phytolacca americana exhibits a range of physiological effects, acting on the skin, glandular structures (especially in the buccal cavity, throat, sexual system, and mammary glands), fibrous and serous tissues, and mucous membranes of the digestive and urinary tracts. It is known to be an alterative, anodyne, anti-inflammatory, antiviral, anticancer, expectorant, emetic, cathartic, narcotic, hypnotic, insecticide, and purgative. The plant's anticancer effects are attributed to its antitumor, anti-inflammatory, and immune-stimulant properties. Certain constituents, such as oleanolic acid, have demonstrated significant anticancer activity against breast, colon, kidney, lung, and pancreatic cancers. The plant also contains antiviral proteins, such as pokeweed antiviral protein (PAP), which have shown potential in inhibiting HIV-1 RNA. Other constituents, including astragalin, ascorbic acid, beta-carotene, and oleanolic acid, contribute to its immune-stimulant and antioxidant properties. Food Uses Despite the toxicity of the seeds within the berries, the berries are sometimes cooked into jelly or pie, with the seeds strained out. Cooking is believed to inactivate the toxins in the berries. The young leaves of the plant are occasionally collected as a spring green and eaten after repeated blanching. Shoots are also blanched and consumed as a substitute for asparagus. However, as the plant matures, it becomes cathartic. Cooked greens are sold commercially in the southern United States, but the use of the plant as food remains controversial due to its toxic components. Toxicity Pokeweed poisonings were common in eastern North America during the 19th century, often resulting from the use of tinctures as antirheumatic preparations or from the ingestion of berries and roots mistaken for parsnip, Jerusalem artichoke, or horseradish. While deaths are now rare, cases of emesis and catharsis still occur. At least one death of a child who consumed crushed seeds in juice has been reported. The toxic components of the plant include saponins based on triterpene genins such as phytolaccagenin, jaligonic acid, phytolaccagenic acid, esculentic acid, and pokeberry genin. These include phytolaccosides A, B, D, E, and G, as well as phytolaccasaponins B, E, and G. Phytolaccigenin is known to cause hemagglutination. Other Uses Pokeberries produce a vibrant purple dye, though it is short-lived and washes out easily. The dye lasts for little more than a month when kept away from sunlight. A patent has been filed to use pokeweed toxins for controlling zebra mussels.
